t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This session covers three questions: the subject of forensic medicine and its tasks, the main tasks of the expert service, and the organisation and structure of the service in Uzbekistan. The student should distinguish forensic medicine as a science from the concept of forensic medical examination, and be able to list the types of examination. The service does not serve only the court and the investigation. It also contributes to improving the quality of treatment and to the prevention of injury, poisoning and sudden death. The service sits within the health care system: the Head Bureau, the regional bureaus and their district and city units. The student should be able to draw this structure.

t: The concept of forensic medicine as a science
n: The concept of forensic medicine as a science. Forensic medicine is a distinct medical science; it studies the medico-biological questions that arise in the work of the court, the investigation and the inquiry. It is not a fundamental but an applied science, closely linked with the medical, legal, natural and philosophical sciences. Examination has four features: it is carried out by a specialist; it addresses a specific task, usually for the purpose of assessment; the procedure is strictly regulated; and the result is formalised in a document. A forensic medical expert differs from a treating physician: he approaches cases not for the purpose of treatment, but for the purpose of legal assessment.

t: Examination and forensic medical examination
n: The concepts of examination and forensic medical examination. According to the definition in Russian law, a forensic examination is a procedural action consisting of conducting a study and giving an opinion on questions that require special knowledge. A forensic medical examination is the resolution, by medical knowledge and in the established manner, of a task set by the investigation and the court; it ends with an expert opinion. An expert is a physician who gives an opinion on questions of medicine and biology. A physician-expert is not a staff member of the expert institution but a physician invited to take part in the case; in rights and duties he is equal to a staff expert. Attention: forensic medicine is a body of knowledge, whereas examination is its practical application.

t: Quick questions: basic concepts
n: Quick questions on the basic concepts. First, remember: forensic medicine as a science is not the forensic medical examination. The science is a body of knowledge, while the examination is the application of that knowledge in practice. First question: name the four features of an expert study, namely the specialist, the specific task, the strict procedure and the document. Second question: who orders a forensic medical examination, and on which questions? Third question: list the four objects of examination: the corpse, living persons, physical evidence and case materials. Try to answer these questions aloud on your own.

t: The subject of forensic medicine
n: The subject of forensic medicine. The subject of the science is the theory and practice of forensic medical examination. The scientific system of the subject was first proposed in 1948 by M.I. Avdeev. The system rests on practice, is linked with the objects of examination, and comprises 8 items. The first group: history and organisational and procedural questions. The second: external factors and examination of the corpse. The third: living persons and physical evidence. The fourth: case materials and examination in cases of professional offences.

t: Content of forensic medicine (component parts)
n: The content of forensic medicine, that is, its component parts. Within the content of the science, thanatology studies death and post-mortem changes, traumatology studies injuries and the mechanism of their formation, and toxicology studies poisons. Obstetrics and gynaecology deals with disputed sexual conditions. Biology and identification study physical evidence and the person. The section on external factors considers the effect of physical factors. Also: the effect of various external factors, and the identification of the person and of the injuring instrument. In 2002 the section on professional offences became a separate subject, “Legal Foundations of a Physician's Practice”.

t: Relation of forensic medicine to other sciences
n: The relation of forensic medicine to other sciences. Forensic medicine is not a fundamental but an applied science; it is linked with the medical, legal, natural and philosophical sciences. The fundamental medical sciences, for example anatomy, histology and physiology, are the foundation of examination; without them an examination cannot be carried out. In some types of examination the clinical sciences are also important, for example traumatology and obstetrics and gynaecology. The legal sciences, that is, criminal and civil law, provide the lawful basis of examination. Chemistry, physics, logic and dialectics ensure that the analysis and conclusions are well founded. The clinician approaches a case for the purpose of treatment, whereas the expert approaches it for the purpose of the legal assessment of the condition.

t: Quick questions: relation of sciences
n: Quick questions on the relation of sciences. First question: knowledge of which clinical science is needed in mechanical injuries? Answer: traumatology. Second question: and in criminal abortion, and in injury to the eye? Obstetrics and gynaecology, and ophthalmology, respectively. Third question: with which science is toxicology linked, and the effects of temperature and electric current? Chemistry and physics. Attention, risk of error! An expert cannot know every specialty in full; he must possess the necessary knowledge from the relevant field. Treatment is not the same as legal assessment.

t: Tasks and significance of forensic medicine
n: The tasks and significance of forensic medicine. Forensic medicine answers the medico-biological questions that arise in court, in the investigation and in the inquiry; its practical application is forensic medical examination. The expert service is part of the health care system; resolving medico-biological questions in criminal and civil cases is its main task. Relying on the materials of examinations, institutions improve the quality of care; prevention of injury, poisoning, sudden death and accidents is carried out. According to a ministerial order, cases are discussed at a clinico-anatomical conference; if the diagnoses do not agree or if shortcomings are found, the head of the institution is notified.

t: Objects and methods of examination
n: The objects and methods of examination. There are four objects: the corpse, the living person, physical evidence, and the materials of criminal and civil cases. The objects are presented by the person who ordered the examination, who is himself responsible for their reliability. Methods fall into three groups. General scientific methods include observation, description and measurement. Particular methods are radiological and chemical. A special method is, for example, comparison of a knife with the injury. A method must be scientific, simple and stable, allow repeated verification, and be documented.

t: Principles of forensic medical examination
n: The principles of forensic medical examination. The principles of the Law “On Forensic Examination”: legality, respect for human rights, independence of the expert, objectivity, comprehensiveness and completeness. An independent expert bears personal responsibility for the study, the result and the opinion, and works only within his competence. An object is a source of evidence only during a certain period: abrasions and bruises are most often examined within the first 10-15 days, and the corpse as soon as possible. Attention: although the expert is independent, his opinion is not binding on the investigator, the prosecutor or the court.

t: Case analysis: science and object
n: Case analysis: science and object. Situation: an abrasion and a bruise were found in a child who came to the polyclinic, and the investigator ordered a forensic medical examination. The object is a living person; medical documents, for example the outpatient record, are also studied as case materials. Method: observation and description, which are general scientific methods; if necessary, a radiological examination, which is a particular method. Time limit: abrasions and bruises are usually examined within 10-15 days. Question: if the investigator asks “who is guilty?”, will the expert answer? Why? Justify this on your own.

t: History of forensic medicine: antiquity and the Middle Ages
n: The history of forensic medicine: antiquity and the Middle Ages. Examination of the corpse in violent death and poisoning was introduced into the rules of Sparta; Hippocrates took part. The laws of Lycurgus date to the 9th-8th century BC. Antistius examined the body of Julius Caesar in 44 BC and, of 23 wounds, judged only one to be the cause of death. The Code of Justinian dates to the 6th century. “Si Yuan Lu” was written in China in 1247; it covered examination of the corpse, weapons, strangulation, drowning and poisoning.

t: History of forensic medicine: formation of the science in Europe
n: The history of forensic medicine: formation of the science in Europe. In the 13th century in Bologna the physician Hugo of Lucca gave opinions in the tribunal. In the 14th century in France “royal surgeons” were appointed, and in Montpellier the corpse was officially examined. The “Carolina” in 1532 made the participation of a physician mandatory in cases of murder, poisoning and miscarriage. Paré's works contain descriptions of wounds, carbon monoxide and lightning, and examples of opinions. At the turn of the 16th-17th century the science began to emerge as a separate field: Schreyer applied the lung test, and Bohn proposed calling the science “forensic medicine”. In the 18th and early 19th century it was taught together with anatomy and surgery. In the 19th century scientists such as Virchow, Rokitansky, Hofmann, Brouardel and Orfila worked in the field.

t: Contribution of Russian and Eastern scientists
n: The contribution of Russian and Eastern scientists. Peter I's “Military Regulations” of 1716 prescribed examination of the bodies of persons who had died a violent death. Pirogov dissected 11,000 corpses and described the entrance hole of a bullet wound. Minakov described subendocardial haemorrhages in persons who died of blood loss, that is, Minakov's spots; Chistovich in 1899 proposed the blood protein reaction. N.S. Bokarius devised a test to establish the vitality of the strangulation furrow. M.I. Raysky defended a dissertation on death from cold. Until the early 20th century the courts in Central Asia were based on Sharia. The works of Biruni and Ibn Sina contain information relevant to forensic medicine, but they were written for therapeutic purposes.

t: Development of forensic medicine in Uzbekistan
n: The development of forensic medicine in Uzbekistan. Departments were established in succession: at the Turkestan University in 1920, at the Samarkand Institute in 1935, at the Andijan Institute in 1959, and at the Tashkent Paediatric Institute in 1972. In 1993 a forensic medicine course was opened at the Tashkent Institute for the Advanced Training of Physicians. Today 9 departments of forensic medicine operate in the higher medical education system. A.S. Ilyin headed the department in 1922-1928; I.V. Markovin became the first chief forensic medical expert in 1930.

t: Quick questions: chronology of history
n: Quick questions on the chronology of history. First question: in which year and by whom was “Si Yuan Lu” published? Answer: 1247, Song Ci, China. Second question: in which year and during whose reign was the “Carolina” code of laws drawn up? Answer: 1532, Charles V, Germany. Third question: where and when was the first department of forensic medicine in Uzbekistan established? Answer: 1920, Turkestan University. Attention: Paré is not Pirogov. Paré was a 16th-century French surgeon; Pirogov was a Russian scientist, author of an atlas of corpse examination, 1846.

t: Case analysis: history and present practice
n: Case analysis: history and present practice. After Julius Caesar was killed in 44 BC, his body was examined by the physician Antistius. Antistius judged that of the 23 wounds on the body only one had led to death. Even now an expert opinion has no binding force in advance: it is assessed alongside other evidence, and if it is rejected, the reason must be justified. Question: in which cases is establishing the cause of death mandatory today, and how does the court treat the expert's opinion? Try to answer this question on your own.

t: Four periods of the service in Uzbekistan
n: The four periods of the service in Uzbekistan. Four periods are conventionally distinguished in the formation and development of the service. Period I, up to the 1920s: episodic examinations; forensic physicians followed the Russian statute of 1842, and there was no expert institution. Period II, up to the 1950s: on the basis of departments, with an office in 1945. Period III, 1950-1991: the Head Bureau and regional bureaus. Period IV, from 1991: an independent state service. Attention: in period II examinations were carried out by departments, in period III by bureaus; do not confuse them.

t: Reforms of the independence period
n: Reforms of the independence period. In the years of independence, the formation of a democratic state and a society based on law set new tasks for the service. The question of fully, properly and promptly meeting the need of law enforcement bodies for examination became pressing. Laws, instructions, rules and standards of examination were developed; for the first time the Law “On Forensic Examination” was adopted. The structure of institutions was improved and new units were opened. A system of training, advanced training and certification of personnel was established.

t: Main tasks of the forensic medical expert service
n: The main tasks of the forensic medical expert service. The main task is to resolve the medico-biological questions that arise in inquiry, investigation and trial in criminal and civil cases, that is, to carry out examination. The service is a specialised branch of the health care system, and its activity differs from other fields in its particular features. On the basis of examination materials, measures aimed at improving the quality of medical care provided to the population must also be carried out. In addition, measures are taken to prevent types of injury, poisoning, sudden death and other accidents.

t: Case analysis: tasks of the service
n: Case analysis: tasks of the service. Situation, a teaching example: a child died suddenly, and the clinical and pathological diagnoses did not agree. According to an order of the Ministry of Health, expert service staff regularly discuss such cases at a clinico-anatomical conference. If the diagnoses do not agree or if there are shortcomings in medical care, the head of the treatment institution is notified in good time. Question: is the expert's task only to establish the cause of death? What recommendations are developed for the prevention of sudden death? Give your answer on the basis of the tasks of the service.

t: Procedural foundations: legal terms
n: Procedural foundations: legal terms. Law is a system of rules, guaranteed by the state and binding on all, that regulates social relations. A statute, in the broad sense, is a normative act binding on everyone. A code is a systematised collection of legal norms of a particular field, that is, the body of laws of that field. The Criminal Code defines crime and punishment. The Code of Criminal Procedure, that is, the CCP, sets the procedure for consideration at the investigation and in court; examination is most often ordered in this process. Examination is carried out on the basis of a ruling of the body of inquiry or investigation, or a ruling of the court. Attention: a “qaror” (ruling) is issued at the investigation, and an “ajrim” (court ruling) in court.

t: Cases of mandatory examination (CCP Article 173)
n: Cases of mandatory examination, Article 173 of the CCP. Article 173 of the CCP lists the cases in which ordering and carrying out an examination is mandatory. These are: the cause of death, the nature and severity of injury, sexual intercourse, signs of pregnancy and abortion, the age of a person where documents are absent or doubtful, and the physical condition of the suspect, the victim and the witness. The necessity and possibility of treating persons infected with a venereal or other infectious disease are also determined. Attention: the list is not closed; examination is also ordered in other cases that require special knowledge.

t: Place of examination and court proceedings
n: The place of examination and court proceedings. Depending on the place, an examination is carried out in the bureau or outside the bureau. In the bureau the conditions are provided by the head of the institution, and outside it by the person who ordered the examination. In the mixed variant the study is carried out partly in the bureau and partly outside; in exhumation the body is opened at the cemetery and the material is examined in the bureau's laboratory. At the court hearing the examination is carried out by experts who gave an opinion at the preliminary investigation or who were appointed by the court. The court issues a ruling and reads it out at the hearing. At the judicial investigation, unlike the preliminary investigation, the expert takes full part in the hearing, asks questions, reads out his opinion and may then be examined.

t: Types of examination
n: The types of examination. The type is chosen according to the reason for ordering it: primary, additional, repeat, commission, complex. In a primary examination the object is examined for the first time, usually by one expert. An additional examination is ordered when the previous opinion has shortcomings or gaps, and is usually performed by the previous expert. A repeat examination is ordered when the opinion is unfounded or doubtful, and is usually carried out by 2 or more experts. A commission examination is held in cases of professional offence, age determination and complex cases. A complex examination also requires a non-medical science, for example an automotive technical examination in a road traffic accident. If the experts of a commission agree, a joint opinion is given; if they disagree, separate opinions are given.

t: Rules of repeat and commission examination
n: Rules of repeat and commission examination. A repeat examination is ordered if the opinion is not substantiated or is doubtful, if the evidence is found unreliable, or if procedural rules are seriously violated. Disagreement of the parties is not grounds for a repeat examination; the reasons for disagreement are stated in the ruling. The previous expert does not perform it. Repeat, commission and complex examinations are carried out only in the appropriate department of the bureau; they are prohibited in the morphological department, the outpatient unit, and district and city units. Attention: an additional examination fills shortcomings and gaps, whereas a repeat examination is carried out again because of doubt about the correctness of the opinion.

t: Case analysis: which examination is ordered?
n: Which examination is ordered: case analysis. Situation: a person was injured in a complex road traffic accident. The opinions of two examinations differ, and the victim's relatives are dissatisfied with the first. If, in such complex accidents, non-medical knowledge is also needed, a forensic medical and automotive technical complex examination may be ordered. A repeat examination is ordered if the opinion is unsubstantiated or its correctness is in doubt; the parties' disagreement alone is not sufficient grounds. Question: which type of examination is appropriate and why? If the court does not agree with the expert's opinion, it must justify this in its ruling.

t: Expert and specialist: rights and duties
n: Expert and specialist: rights and duties. The expert assesses a medical fact, gives an opinion and draws up the expert's report; he takes part in the examination, in questioning and in the court hearing. The specialist helps in finding evidence and does not draw up an independent document; he takes part in inspection and exhumation. The expert's rights: to become familiar with the case materials, to request additional materials, to give an opinion in his native language, and to lodge a complaint. Criminal liability: a knowingly false opinion, Article 238; disclosure of information, Article 239; refusal to give an opinion, Article 240. Attention: a person who was previously a specialist in the case may later be an expert. A challenge is resolved at the investigation within 24 hours.

t: Expert opinion and documents
n: The expert opinion and documents. The opinion consists of an introductory part, a research part and a conclusion. The introduction states the date, the grounds and the questions; the research part gives the method and results; the conclusion gives clear answers to the questions. The research part is written in language understandable to a person without special knowledge. At the end the investigator and the court assess the opinion. The act is drawn up on the basis of a referral: a receipt of rights is not taken, and its final part is called the “conclusion”. The opinion has no probative force in advance. Disagreement with it must be justified in the ruling.

t: Types of witness: professional and expert
n: Types of witness: professional and expert. According to Simpson, this section distinguishes two roles. A professional witness gives factual medical evidence: for example, an emergency physician confirms the presence of a fracture or a wound. He does not usually give opinions, and the report states only the findings. An expert witness gives an opinion on medical facts: for example, on the cause of a fracture or a wound. The two roles often merge: a forensic pathologist prepares a report on his own examination, then gives an opinion and interpretation. The expert's task is to give an objective, impartial assessment or interpretation of the evidence under consideration.

t: Duties of the expert (Simpson, England and Wales)
n: The duties of the expert, according to Simpson, practice in England and Wales. The expert's evidence must be, and must appear to be, independent of and uninfluenced by the demands of the court proceedings. The expert never assumes the role of an advocate; he states clearly the facts or assumptions on which his opinion is based. If a question lies outside his expertise, he says so; if the data are insufficient, he indicates that his opinion is provisional. After receiving new data or the opinion of another expert, he is ready to reconsider his opinion and, if necessary, to change it. These rules are called the Ikarian Reefer and Anglo Group rules.

t: Procedure for giving evidence in court (England and Wales)
n: The procedure for giving evidence in court, England and Wales. The first stage is the oath: each witness swears to tell the truth or makes a solemn promise, that is, an affirmation; after that, liability for false evidence arises. The second stage is the main questioning: first the party that called the witness questions him, which is examination in chief. The third stage is cross-questioning: the advocates of the other side question the witness, which is cross-examination. The fourth stage is re-questioning: the first advocate clarifies the matters raised in cross-examination, which is re-examination, but he cannot open a new topic. The judge may ask a clarifying question at any time; most judges wait until the end of re-examination.

t: Conduct of the expert in court and the report (England and Wales)
n: The conduct of the expert in court and the report, England and Wales. Testimony is given clearly, objectively and without emotion; the oath or solemn promise is spoken in a clear voice. It is right to say “I don't know” to a question one cannot answer, or not to answer a question outside one's competence. A witness under oath must not be irritable or rude; to a complex question one may decline to answer only “yes” or “no”. In preparing a report, one first checks one's specialty and competence, then the written consent or legal basis. Next one relies on the initial notes made at the time of the examination, and the facts are checked before signing.

t: Quick questions: opinion and liability
n: Quick questions on the opinion and liability. First question: is the expert's opinion binding on the court and the investigator? No: if they disagree, they justify this in the ruling. The opinion has three parts: introductory, research and concluding, that is, the conclusion part. The expert does not collect materials independently and does not report the result to anyone other than the body that ordered the examination. Criminal liability is provided for a knowingly false opinion under Article 238, for disclosure of information under Article 239, and for refusal to give an opinion under Article 240.

t: Organisation of forensic medical examination in Uzbekistan
n: The organisation of forensic medical examination in Uzbekistan. The main service is within the system of the Ministry of Health; matters concerning military personnel are handled by the service of the Ministry of Defence. The system: the Head Bureau, regional bureaus and their district, inter-district and city units. There are 13 regional institutions, that is, Karakalpakstan and the regions; their structure is identical. In administrative and financial matters they are subordinate to the regional health authority. In organisational, methodological and expert matters they are subordinate to the Head Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination. District, inter-district and city units are subordinate to the regional bureau.

t: Structure and departments of the bureau
n: The structure and departments of the bureau. The morphological department, together with the forensic histology department, performs examination of the corpse and microscopy. The forensic medical outpatient unit examines living persons. The repeat and commission department carries out repeat, commission and complex examinations. The department of medical criminalistics studies the mechanism of injury, the instrument and the person. Forensic chemistry deals with toxicological examination, and forensic biology with physical evidence such as blood, hair and stains. The organisational and methodological department coordinates the work of the other structures and provides methodological support. Attention: repeat, commission and complex examinations are not carried out in outpatient and district units.

t: Case analysis: structure of the bureau
n: Case analysis: structure of the bureau. Situation: a bloodstain on clothing and material from a corpse arrived at the bureau. Question: in which departments are they examined, and can the head of the bureau change the opinion? Blood, secretions and their stains, tissue and hair, as physical evidence, are examined in the forensic biology department. To detect poison, a toxicological examination of biological material is needed: it takes place in the forensic chemistry department. Microscopic examination is carried out in the forensic histology department. Attention: the head of the bureau is not the author of the opinion. He points out shortcomings but cannot cancel the opinion; only the expert who gave it is responsible for it.

t: Conclusion: key takeaways and self-assessment
n: Conclusion. Forensic medicine answers the medico-biological questions that arise in court and in the investigation; examination is its practical application and ends with an opinion. The types of examination: primary, additional, repeat, commission, complex. The opinion consists of an introductory part, a research part and a concluding part, that is, the conclusion. The service is within the system of the Ministry of Health: the Head Bureau, 13 regional bureaus and units. The bureaus have morphological, forensic chemistry and forensic biology departments. Homework: combine into one table the rights and duties of the expert and the specialist, the grounds for challenge, and the departments of the bureau.
